meta.description: Not Dostoevsky. The line is the closing couplet of Apollon Maykov's 1878 Russian poem “Ne govori, chto net spasenya” — misattributed online for years.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The darker the night, the brighter the stars, the deeper the grief, the closer is God!'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dostoevsky. It's the closing couplet of Apollon Maykov's 1878 Russian poem — Wikiquote files the Dostoevsky credit under Misattributed.

answer.label: Not Fyodor Dostoevsky — actually Apollon Maykov
answer.sourceLine: These lines are the closing couplet of “Не говори, что нет спасенья” (“Do not say there is no salvation”), a short poem written in 1878 by the Russian poet Apollon Maykov and published in his cycle “From Apollodorus the Gnostic.” The popular English wording faithfully renders Maykov's Russian — “Чем ночь темней, тем ярче звёзды, / Чем глубже скорбь, тем ближе Бог.” It appears nowhere in Dostoevsky; Wikiquote lists the Dostoevsky credit under “Misattributed” ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Не говори, что нет спасенья” (untitled; known by its first line)
1878, in the cycle “Из Аполлодора Гностика” (From Apollodorus the Gnostic)

source.excerpt:
Не говори, что нет спасенья,
Что ты в печалях изнемог:
Чем ночь темней, тем ярче звёзды,
Чем глубже скорбь, тем ближе Бог…

“Do not say there is no salvation, that you are worn out by your griefs: the darker the night, the brighter the stars; the deeper the sorrow, the closer is God…”
trail: Wikiquote files the Dostoevsky credit under “Misattributed” ↗, noting the words come from an untitled 1878 poem by Apollon Maykov, not from Crime and Punishment.
Russian Wikisource carries the primary quatrain ↗, dated 1878 and placed in the cycle “From Apollodorus the Gnostic.”

A parallel Russian/English text on LyricsTranslate ↗ renders the couplet as “the darker the night, the brighter the stars; the deeper the sorrow, the closer to God” — the same lines pinned on Dostoevsky.
source.excerptNote: The famous English quote is just the third and fourth lines of this four-line poem.

source.rightsNote: Maykov's Russian original (1878) is long in the public domain. But the exact English wording circulating online is an anonymous, unattributed translation with no identifiable translator or publication date, so its copyright status cannot be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Apollon Maykov
author.heading: Apollon Maykov, not Dostoevsky
author.bio: Apollon Nikolayevich Maykov (1821–1897) was one of the foremost Russian poets of the generation after Pushkin, known for classical, landscape and religious lyric verse. He published this quatrain in 1878 under the conceit of translating a 2nd-century Gnostic poet, “Apollodorus the Gnostic” — a figure Maykov later admitted he had invented (in Russkaya Starina, 1899), saying he left even philologists believing such a poet existed.

misattribution.heading: How Dostoevsky got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet's most-shared “Dostoevsky” quotes — often sourced to Crime and Punishment. It is not in that novel, nor anywhere in Dostoevsky's fiction, letters or diaries. It belongs to a fellow 19th-century Russian, the poet Apollon Maykov.

items.why: The dominant online credit, frequently tagged to Crime and Punishment. Wikiquote places it under “Misattributed” ↗ and points to Maykov's 1878 poem as the actual source.

Maykov first published these lines as if translated from a 2nd-century Gnostic poet he called Apollodorus ↗ — a figure he later confessed he had invented (in Russkaya Starina, 1899: “Apollodorus the Gnostic is my invention”), which helped obscure the true byline.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are the closing couplet of Apollon Maykov's 1878 poem “Не говори, что нет спасенья,” not a line Dostoevsky ever wrote — see the primary text ↗.

context.heading: A consolation poem, not a novel line
lead: Maykov wrote the quatrain in 1878 as a compact religious consolation: four lines urging that despair is not the last word. Its two closing images — brighter stars in a darker night, God nearer in deeper grief — are what travelled, detached from the poem and, eventually, from their author.

Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was Maykov's close friend and contemporary, which may be why the orphaned lines drifted onto the far more globally famous novelist. But the sentiment and the verse are Maykov's.
detailsBody: Maykov framed several late poems as translations from “Apollodorus the Gnostic,” a supposed 2nd-century poet. He admitted the figure was his own fabrication (in Russkaya Starina, 1899), remarking that he left many readers — even philologists — convinced such a poet had really existed. So the line has, in a sense, two layers of misattribution: to a fictional ancient, then to Dostoevsky.
context.pull: “The darker the night, the brighter the stars” is Maykov consoling, not Raskolnikov confessing.
